kf: **Emollients** restore the skin barrier: the foundation of treatment for eczema, psoriasis, ichthyosis and dry skin.
Types run from lotions (light, more water) through creams and gels to **ointments** (greasiest, most occlusive, fewest preservatives).
Use **liberally and often**: adults with eczema may need about 250–500 g a week; apply in the direction of hair growth.
Use as a **soap substitute**; leave 15–30 minutes between emollient and topical steroid.
**Fire risk**: paraffin-based (and other) emollients dried on fabric are flammable; warn about naked flames and smoking (MHRA).
myths: **"Emollients are just moisturisers, optional"**: regular use reduces flares and steroid use.
**"Aqueous cream is a good emollient"**: it contains sodium lauryl sulfate, an irritant; avoid as a leave-on.
patho_lead: Emollients work by **occluding, humectant attraction of water and replacing lipids**.

mech.t: Oily layers (paraffin, petrolatum) slow transepidermal water loss.
mech.cap: A leaky barrier loses water and lets irritants in; emollients seal it.

mech.t: Urea, glycerol and lactic acid draw water into the stratum corneum.
Ceramides and fatty acids refill gaps between corneocytes.
More oil = more occlusion but less cosmetic acceptability.
mech.cap: Spectrum from light lotions to greasy ointments.

mech.t: Smooth on downwards in the direction of hair growth to avoid folliculitis.

comp: Folliculitis, irritant reactions (preservatives, lanolin), slipping and falls, fire risk.

cf_figs.caption: Emollients range from light lotions to very greasy ointments — the right one is the one the patient will use.
